body: We're not a software factory, and we won't propose building something that already exists in the market. The same agnostic diagnosis we use to select an ERP or CRM is what we apply here: we first evaluate whether the right solution already exists.

When it genuinely doesn't, we know how to build it: process automations and specialized AI agents for tasks within each phase of the CIRA method — diagnosis, vendor evaluation, risk monitoring, adoption measurement — integrated into the enterprise AI architecture we already govern, so it doesn't become one more ownerless tool.

An AI agent is a system that receives a goal and completes a multi-step task on its own: it looks up information in your systems, applies business rules, drafts or updates records, and alerts a person when it needs a decision. It differs from a chatbot in that it doesn't just answer questions: it acts on processes.

Some use cases in companies are classifying and answering incoming requests, preparing and reconciling information across systems, watching indicators and flagging deviations, and assisting a team with repetitive analysis tasks. None of them works well without a clear process behind it and someone inside the organization who is accountable for the result.

This is how we work on an AI agent: first a specific process is chosen and the way the result will be measured is agreed; then we define what the agent can do on its own and what must go through a person's approval; next it's tested with real cases from operations and adjusted; and finally it runs with a clear owner inside the organization. Without that order, an agent impresses in a demo and changes nothing day to day.

An AI agent isn't always the answer. If the process is stable and rule-based, RPA or traditional automation is cheaper and more predictable; if the process isn't defined, it has to be put in order first. Some risks of a poorly designed agent are excessive permissions, wrong answers delivered with confidence, and lack of traceability, which is why we design it together with AI governance.

body: Enterprise architecture defines how an organization's processes, data, and systems connect. Applied to artificial intelligence, it keeps each new tool from being added as an island.

Every area buys its own AI tool with no visibility into what already exists elsewhere in the organization. The result isn't innovation — it's a collection of isolated systems, with no common data governance and real security risk.

We design the architecture layer that connects those models, data, and systems securely and scalably — the same layer that underpins the process automation and AI governance we work on at Cyrrus Intelligence Lab.

An enterprise architecture is organized in three layers: the business processes, the data those processes produce and consume, and the systems that support them. Artificial intelligence sits on top of those three layers: if the data is scattered or the systems don't talk to each other, no model works well, however advanced it is.

That's why data architecture is a central part of the work: defining where each piece of data comes from, who owns it, how it connects across systems, and who can use it. It's the step before any serious AI project, and it avoids redoing integrations every time a new use case is added.

Some signs an organization needs to put its architecture in order: each area buys its own tools, the same figures show up differently in different systems, every new integration takes months, and no one knows for certain what data the AI models touch.

The outcome of the work is a map of the systems, data, and models that exist today, a target architecture that connects them securely and scalably, and a prioritized roadmap to get there without stopping operations.

body: Without a governance framework, every AI initiative is left to the judgment of whoever implemented it. When something goes wrong — sensitive data exposed, an automated decision with no traceability — there's no one to turn to and no way to audit what happened.

We don't start from scratch or stop what already works: we audit the AI already in use in the organization — which tools exist, who bought them, and what data they work with — and bring it into a single framework, instead of asking each area to start over.

With that inventory, leadership makes four decisions (Cyrrus's judgment): which framework to use as the reference and for what — managing risk (NIST), setting values (OECD), or certifying a management system (ISO/IEC 42001), which can be combined —, who is accountable for AI in the company, what evidence to keep for each decision, and how often to review it all.

AI governance rests on data governance: what information a model can touch, what stays out of scope, and who owns each piece of data. That's why data controls are part of the framework, not a separate project.
This framework runs transversally beneath the CIRA method's four phases, so every AI decision — from diagnosis to adoption — stays documented and auditable.

items.question: Which AI governance framework should we use: NIST, OECD, or ISO/IEC 42001?
items.answer: It depends on what you need it for (Cyrrus's judgment): the NIST AI RMF is for managing risk, the OECD principles for setting values, and the ISO/IEC 42001 standard for implementing and certifying an AI management system. They aren't mutually exclusive and can be combined.

items.question: What's the difference between AI governance and data governance?
items.answer: Data governance defines where each piece of data comes from, who owns it, and who can use it. AI governance rests on it and adds who approves each AI use case, which data a model can touch, and who audits its decisions. At Cyrrus we work on both together.

items.question: What AI governance evidence do you have to present to a client or a regulator?

items.question: Does AI governance slow down innovation inside the company?
items.answer: The goal isn't slower approval — it's approval with judgment. With clear rules for what's in and what's out, approval can be faster.

body: Data governance solves a problem recognized in the first board meeting: two departments present different figures for the same indicator and the discussion turns into which number is true, not what to do about it.

Defining data governance means deciding, for each domain (customers, products, finance, people), who owns the data, which system the official version comes from, which quality rules apply when it is captured and who may use it. These are leadership decisions, not system settings.

We don't start from scratch or propose a year-long project: we audit the data the company already has — which systems generate it, where it is duplicated, which figures don't reconcile — and define the rules on the systems already in production. The CRM and the ERP are a frequent starting point in our projects, because that is where customers, sales and finance live.

Data governance is the foundation of AI governance: a model is only auditable if it is known which data it used, where it came from and who answered for its quality. That is why data controls for AI — what a model may touch and what it may not — are defined here and integrated into the AI governance framework, not as a separate project.

The DAMA-DMBOK, published by DAMA International, is the recognized reference framework for data management and serves as a guide to structure functions and responsibilities. In our view, a midsize company doesn't need to implement all of it: it needs clear owners, a catalog of critical data and rules that are followed in the systems it already uses. To prepare leadership we offer the data governance for executives workshop at Leadership Academy.

items.answer: No. Data quality (completeness, duplicates, validity) is one of the outcomes of governance. Governance defines who answers for that quality, under which rules and in which system; without owners, data cleanup repeats every year.

items.question: Do we need a data governance tool?
items.answer: Not at first. Capture, deduplication and access rules are applied first in the systems that already exist (CRM, ERP). A catalog or quality tool is evaluated later, with the same vendor-independent criteria we use in every selection.

items.question: What deliverables does data governance consulting with Cyrrus leave?
items.answer: A data assessment, the governance model (domains, owners, committee), the quality and access policies, the catalog of critical data with its lineage and the data controls for AI, plus the adoption plan.

items.question: What is leadership's role in data governance?
items.answer: It decides who owns each domain, which indicator is the official one and which data stays out of AI's reach. The data governance for executives workshop at Leadership Academy prepares those decisions.

respuesta.title: What is AI strategy consulting?
respuesta.body: It is the service that turns interest in artificial intelligence into a roadmap: which business processes can change with AI, how much changing them is worth, which data and systems are needed and what governance makes them auditable. At Cyrrus the AI strategy is built on three pillars we already work on: AI governance, architecture and automation with agents.

body: An AI strategy answers three questions: in which processes AI changes a business outcome, in what order it's worth doing, and what it takes — data, systems, governance — for it to work in production and not only in a demonstration.

That is why we don't start with the tool. First we inventory the AI already in use in the organization and the data that exists; then, with the departments, we identify candidate processes and prioritize them with a single criterion: impact, feasibility, data and risk. The result is a short list leadership can approve or reject with the same criteria.

Each use case in the roadmap carries how it will be measured: against the real process it replaces — time, errors, cost — and not against the demo. It is the same criterion we use to execute automation with AI agents, so strategy and execution use the same yardstick.

The AI strategy rests on governance and architecture: which data each model may touch, who approves and audits, and which systems it connects to. Defining it in the strategy prevents, in our view, two failures we see in our projects: pilots that can't move to production for lack of data, and tools bought by five departments that don't talk to each other.

This service is the entry point to Cyrrus Intelligence Lab and connects with the IT strategy of the CIRA method's Construct phase: AI is one more initiative in the technology portfolio, with its business case, not a separate project. To prepare the committee we offer the AI for executives workshop at Leadership Academy.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions about AI strategy consulting

items.question: When should a company hire AI strategy consulting services?
items.answer: When the committee receives AI proposals and has no criteria to compare them; when several departments have already bought tools on their own; when a pilot worked in a demo and didn't move to production; or when the board asks for an AI plan with benefits, costs and risks before approving a budget.

items.question: What is the difference between AI strategy and AI governance?
items.answer: The strategy decides which use cases are done, in what order and with what measurement. Governance defines the policies, roles and controls they are executed and audited with. Strategy without governance produces unauditable pilots; governance without strategy produces rules for initiatives no one prioritized. At Cyrrus they are worked on together.

items.question: What deliverables does AI strategy consulting with Cyrrus leave?
items.answer: An inventory of existing AI, a list of prioritized use cases with their criteria, a roadmap with sequence and owners, data and architecture requirements, the applicable governance framework and the measurement plan for each case.

items.question: Do you recommend specific AI tools or models?
items.answer: Only after defining the use case, the data and the governance. AI and automation platform selection is done with the same vendor-independent criteria we use in every solution selection.

items.question: How do you measure whether the AI strategy worked?
items.answer: Case by case, against the real process it changes: time, errors, cost or revenue of the process before and after. That criterion is defined in the strategy and applied when the case is executed.

items.question: What is leadership's role in the AI strategy?
items.answer: Approving the prioritized list, deciding the governance framework and the data AI may not touch, and reviewing the measurement. The AI for executives workshop at Leadership Academy prepares those decisions.
